title: Concurrent loss of LKB1 and KEAP1 enhances SHMT-mediated antioxidant defence in KRAS-mutant lung cancer
author: Hyun Min Lee; Nefertiti Muhammad; Elizabeth L Lieu; Feng Cai; Jiawei Mu; Yun-Sok Ha; Guoshen Cao; Chamey Suchors; Kenneth Joves; Constantinos Chronis; Kailong Li; Gregory S Ducker; Kellen Olszewski; Ling Cai; Derek B Allison; Sara E Bachert; William R Ewing; Harvey Wong; Hyosun Seo; Isaac Y Kim; Brandon Faubert; James Kim; Jiyeon Kim
text:
Abstract
Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with concurrent mutations in KRAS and the tumour suppressor LKB1 (KL NSCLC) is refractory to most therapies and has one of the worst predicted outcomes. Here we describe a KL-induced metabolic vulnerability associated with serine–glycine-one-carbon (SGOC) metabolism. Using RNA-seq and metabolomics data from human NSCLC, we uncovered that LKB1 loss enhanced SGOC metabolism via serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT). LKB1 loss, in collaboration with KEAP1 loss, activated SHMT through inactivation of the salt-induced kinase (SIK)–NRF2 axis and satisfied the increased demand for one-carbon units necessary for antioxidant defence. Chemical and genetic SHMT suppression increased cellular sensitivity to oxidative stress and cell death. Further, the SHMT inhibitor enhanced the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of paclitaxel (first-line NSCLC therapy inducing oxidative stress) in KEAP1-mutant KL tumours. The data reveal how this highly aggressive molecular subtype of NSCLC fulfills their metabolic requirements and provides insight into therapeutic strategies.
Tumours develop metabolic phenotypes distinct from those of adjacent, non-malignant tissues, to support energy production, biosynthetic activity and resistance to metabolic stress. The most common metabolic alterations include enhancement of aerobic glycolysis1, glutaminolysis2, and mitochondrial biogenesis and functions3, all of which are often associated with oncogene activation and/or loss of function of tumour suppressors. For example, MYC overexpression stimulates glycolysis and glutamine catabolism by transactivating glucose-transporter genes, glycolytic genes4,5 and genes associated with glutamine transport and glutaminase activity6,7. Oncogenic KRAS accommodates the increased demand for nutrients to support cell proliferation by enhancing fatty-acid uptake, glucose uptake and glycolysis; stimulating glutamine catabolism and inducing catabolic processes, including autophagy and macropinocytosis; and modulating redox balance8–12. Tumour suppressor LKB1 (encoded by STK11) acts as a metabolic energy sensor to regulate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and other kinases during periods of energetic stress. The LKB1–AMPK pathway suppresses mTOR complex 1 signalling, resetting the balance between energy production and use13–15.
Given the important roles of tumour suppressors and oncogenes in metabolic reprogramming, there is significant translational potential in identifying and understanding how particular oncogenotypes influence tumor metabolism, and whether these changes impose liabilities that can be exploited therapeutically. In more recent studies, however, a nuanced picture has emerged, showing that tissue context impacts the execution of metabolic reprogramming, even with the same oncogenic drivers. MYC induces metabolic changes in both lung and liver tumours but activates glutamine catabolism in lung tumours and glutamine synthesis in liver tumours16. Differences in branched chain amino acid (BCAA) metabolism between pancreatic cancer and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) driven by the same driver mutations are another prime example: LUAD tumours have increased uptake of BCAAs, which are used as a nitrogen source, whereas pancreatic tumours have decreased BCAA uptake17. Thus, understanding how the cell of origin interacts with genetic events to affect the metabolic dependence of tumours will be critical for selecting the right treatment approaches.
In this study, we analysed the metabolome of surgically resected human NSCLC samples and compared those with KRAS mutations (K) with those with KL mutations. We demonstrate that SGOC metabolism is the most significantly altered metabolic pathway in KL NSCLC, similar to what occurs in pancreatic KL tumour models18. Through further metabolic analyses, however, we reveal the differences in SGOC metabolism between these two tumour types. Whereas KL pancreatic tumours require SGOC metabolism for DNA methylation18, KL NSCLC depends on SGOC metabolism through SHMT enzymes to maintain redox homeostasis. Notably, such SHMT dependence is associated with the concurrent mutation of KEAP1 (KLK oncogenotype). Suppressing either SHMT1 or SHMT2 readily induces production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and impedes viability of KLK NSCLC. This is distinct from other cancer settings, in which deletion of either SHMT isoform is insufficient to inhibit cell proliferation under nutrient-replete conditions19–21. Finally, we demonstrate that inhibiting SHMT in combination with treatment with a ROS-inducing chemotherapeutic agent reduces tumour growth in vivo. The dependence of KLK NSCLC on SHMT for antioxidant defence suggests a metabolic vulnerability that can be explored as a new therapeutic strategy for this highly aggressive subtype of NSCLC.
Results
LKB1 loss enhances serine–glycine biosynthesis in NSCLC
In previous studies, we have demonstrated that KL NSCLC displays hallmarks of altered metabolism of nitrogen handling22–24. To more comprehensively investigate metabolic pathways that are highly perturbed and might be actionable targets in human KL NSCLC, we compared the metabolome of KL tumours with that of K tumours using a human NSCLC tumour metabolomics dataset that we previously generated22. Metabolite set enrichment analysis25,26 revealed a strong enrichment of folate and methionine cycles, which are closely associated with SGOC metabolism (Fig. 1a,c and Supplementary Tables 1 and 4). Direct inspection of levels of individual metabolites related to the folate–methionine cycle or SGOC metabolism also revealed that several were significantly altered in KL tumours (Fig. 1b, log2(fold change) > 1 or < –1). Metabolomics analysis of an isogenic pair of A549 cells, a KL cell line derived from human NSCLC, with or without LKB1 overexpression (A549-empty vector (EV) and A549-LKB1 cells) further validated that alterations in levels of metabolites related to the folate–methionine cycle or SGOC metabolism are associated with LKB1 status (Supplementary Tables 2, 3 and 5 and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Given the close link between the folate–methionine cycle and SGOC metabolism, as well as its critical role in cancer survival and growth, further study of SGOC metabolism was prioritized.
These results raised questions about the role of LKB1 in SGOC metabolism. To understand the relationships between LKB1 loss and SGOC metabolism, we assessed cellular sensitivity to serine and glycine deprivation. LKB1 loss conferred resistance to serine and glycine deprivation, whereas expression of wild-type (WT) LKB1, but not kinase-dead (KD) LKB1, sensitized cells to it, suggesting that LKB1 inhibits serine and glycine biosynthesis through its downstream kinase(s) activity (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1j). Serine and glycine are non-essential amino acids and can be synthesized de novo from glycolytic intermediate 3-phospho-D-glycerate (3PG). To assess the flow of serine and glycine biosynthesis, we measured incorporation of 13C originating from universally labelled glucose ([U-13C]glucose) into serine and glycine. Genetically engineered KL cells and NSCLC cells harbouring KL mutations that arose naturally both displayed higher fractions of serine m + 3 and glycine m + 2, and the size of the serine and glycine pools was not significantly affected (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1c–e,g–i; the KL mutation status of cell lines is available in Supplementary Table 9). Similarly, KL cells exhibited higher labelling in serine derived from amine-nitrogen-labelled glutamine ([α-15N]glutamine) (Fig. 1g).
Serine hydroxymethyltransferase 1 (cytosolic) and 2 (mitochondrial) (SHMT1 and SHMT2) catalyse the conversion of serine and tetrahydrofolate (THF) into glycine and 5,10-methylene-THF. We assessed the flow of glycine synthesis from serine by measuring the incorporation of 13C originating from [U-13C]serine into glycine. There was little difference in serine uptake (Fig. 1h, left, and Extended Data Fig. 1k) between K and KL cells, indicating that LKB1 status does not affect serine uptake. However, KL cells (A549, H460, H2122, H157 and H1355) exhibited a higher baseline fractional enrichment of glycine m + 2 than did K cells (H1373), whereas LKB1 expression reduced levels of serine-to-glycine conversion in KL cells, and LKB1 silencing increased the glycine m + 2 fraction in K cells (Fig. 1h, right,i and Extended Data Fig. 1l). The ratios of M + 2 to M + 1 serine from [U-13C]serine labelling can offer insights into the serine-cycling rates; a lower M + 2/M + 1 ratio (increased portion of M + 1 mass isotopologue) indicates more active one-carbon cycling. LKB1 expression increases the serine m + 2/m + 1 ratio from [U-13C]serine, however, further supporting the idea that LKB1 limits folate-dependent serine metabolism and thus inhibits one-carbon cycling (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Notably, carbon from both [U-13C]glucose-derived serine and [U-13C]serine was readily metabolized into glycine m + 2, and LKB1 loss increased 13C enrichment of glycine in both settings (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 1d,e,i,l), indicating that the serine contribution from both de novo biosynthesis and extracellular sources to the one-carbon pool is facilitated by LKB1 loss.
LKB1 in NSCLC regulates SHMT expression through SIK1
LKB1 has been reported to suppress gene expression of multiple enzymes in the serine synthesis pathway enzymes through AMPK in a KRAS-driven murine pancreatic-cancer model18. Similar to pancreatic-cancer settings, LKB1 loss in human NSCLC cell lines also upregulated expression of serine pathway enzymes (PHGDH, PSAT1, SHMT1 and SHMT2), whereas restoration of LKB1 expression reversed these changes (Extended Data Fig. 2a–d). In human NSCLC tissues, however, only expression levels of SHMT1—and, to a lesser extent, SHMT2—exhibited a correlation with LKB1 mutation status (Fig. 2a; participants’ KL and P53 mutation status is available in Supplementary Table 10, and statistical analysis in Supplementary Table 6). PHGDH and PSAT1 expression levels also seem to be linked to LKB1 status (L versus K versus KL); no difference was observed when compared with the WT tumour group. Because we sought to determine a potentially actionable target in human KL NSCLC, we directed our focus to how SHMTs are regulated and impact tumours with KL mutations (Fig. 2b).
First, to evaluate whether AMPK, similar to its role in pancreatic KL tumour models18, acts as a key downstream effector to suppress SHMT expression in NSCLC, we silenced AMPKα1 and AMPKα2 in a panel of isogenic pairs of cell lines with either K or KL mutations. Although AMPK suppression completely restored expression of the first two enzymes of the serine-biosynthesis pathway (PHGDH and PSAT1) and, to a lesser extent, SHMT2, it did not restore SHMT1 expression in K mutant settings (Extended Data Fig. 2e–h). Accordingly, mTOR inhibition, assessed using Torin 1 as a readout of AMPK activation18, fully reduced expression of PHGDH and PSAT1, and partially reduced that of SHMT2, but did not affect SHMT1 (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j), suggesting that the AMPK–mTORC1 axis might not be a major regulator of SHMT expression in KL NSCLC.
Of 12 other LKB1 downstream kinases that are closely related to AMPK, salt-induced kinases (SIKs) have emerged as key regulators of metabolism through transcriptional control27,28. Given that recent studies have shown that the LKB1–SIK axis is critical for tumour growth and aggressiveness in NSCLC29–31, we reasoned that SIK might suppress SHMT expression. RNA interference (RNAi) silencing and CRISPR-knockout (KO) of SIK1 and SIK3 increased both SHMT1 and SHMT2 gene expression, but not PHGDH and PSAT1 expression, even in the presence of LKB1 (Extended Data Fig. 2k–o). This result implies that gene expression of components of the serine biosynthesis pathway (PHGDH and PSAT1) and serine entry into one-carbon metabolism (SHMT1 and SHMT2) are differentially regulated in NSCLC. Among the SIK isoforms (SIK1–SIK3), SIK1 has been implicated to have a primary tumour-suppressive role in NSCLC29,30. Consistent with previous reports, SIK1 deletion was sufficient to restore SHMT expression (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2p), which was reversed with expression of SIK1 (Extended Data Fig. 2q), suggesting that there is potentially a link between SIK1’s tumour-suppressive function and its role in regulating SHMT expression. Notably, although SIK suppression completely reconstituted SHMT expression at the level of transcription, mRNA recovery did not fully translate into restored protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 2l), indicating that there might be another layer of signalling that controls SHMT protein levels.
SIK1 regulates SHMT through the NRF2–MAFK axis
Next, we sought to define the mechanism by which SIK regulates SHMT gene expression. SIK has been known to regulate metabolism by controlling gene expression through direct inhibitory phosphorylation of transcriptional regulators and transcriptional coactivators, including class IIa histone deacetylases (HDACs) and the CREB-regulated transcriptional coactivators (CRTCs)32. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2; encoded by NFE2L2) controls gene expression of SGOC-metabolism enzymes through activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), the transcriptional master regulator of amino-acid metabolism33, raising the possibility that SIK inhibits ATF4-mediated transactivation of SHMT. ATF4 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by qPCR (ChIP–qPCR) revealed strong binding of ATF4 to the SHMT2 promoter, which was reduced by LKB1 but restored by SIK inhibition (Fig. 2e). Binding of ATF4 to the SHMT1 promoter, however, was relatively weak (Fig. 2e), suggesting that (1) expression levels of SHMT1 and SHMT2 can be differentially regulated, and (2) additional factors might control SHMT1 expression.
To investigate the epigenetic landscape around the SHMT locus and identify possible regulatory transcription factor(s) for SHMT, we performed the assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) on H460 (KL) cells. ATAC-seq identified accessible chromatin around the transcription start sites (TSSs) of the SHMT genes, consistent with their expression in H460. The boundaries of the identified open chromatin region that includes the putative SHMT promoter were scanned using HOMER34 to identify footprints that predict transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) (Fig. 2f). Notably, multiple NRF-binding motifs, including the antioxidant response element (ARE), were identified in the SHMT1 promoter region. The SHMT2 active promoter also contained one NRF-binding motif. Because these binding sites are located in DNA footprint regions, it is highly likely that members of the NRF family of transcription factors can directly bind to the SHMT promoters and regulate transcription.
NRF2 binds to AREs as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins, of which there are three: MAFF, MAFG and MAFK35. ChIP–seq data (acetylated histone H3 K27 (H3K27ac) ChIP: GSM1003578; MAFK ChIP: GSE127353; trimethylated histone H3 K4 (H3K4me3) ChIP: GSM2421528) of SHMT1 and SHMT2 loci in A549 (KL) cells revealed that MAFK bound to the promoter regions of both genes (Extended Data Fig. 3a), supporting the idea of NRF2–MAFK-mediated transactivation of SHMT. Consistent with the ChIP–seq and ATAC-seq data, ChIP–qPCR revealed that both MAFK and NRF2 directly bound to SHMT1 and SHMT2 promoter regions, and these binding levels were reduced by LKB1 expression and restored by SIK inhibition (Fig. 2g and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Binding of both NRF2 and MAFK to SHMT1 promoter regions was more readily recovered by SIK inhibition than was NRF2 and MAFK binding to the SHMT2 promoter, consistent with our results showing that expression levels of SHMT1 and SHMT2 are differentially regulated (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 2e,i).
Silencing MAFK decreased both SHMT1 and SHMT2 mRNA expression (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 3c). Luciferase reporter assays also revealed that both genetic and pharmacological suppression of SIK enhanced luciferase activity of WT SHMT1 and SHMT2 promoters (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 3d–f,i), whereas SIK1 overexpression significantly attenuated luciferase activity (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). Accordingly, SIK suppression increased SHMT activity and one-carbon cycling in K settings, as determined by 13C incorporation from [U-13C] serine to the m + 2 glycine isotopologue (Fig. 2k–m and Extended Data Fig. 3m,o) and the serine m + 2/m + 1 ratio from [U-13C]serine (Extended Data Fig. 3n,p), respectively. Neither AMPK deletion nor AMPK activation affected SHMT activity (Extended Data Fig. 3j–l), further confirming that SIK, rather than AMPK, is the key downstream effector of LKB1 that regulates SHMT expression and activity. Collectively, our data imply that SIK—mainly SIK1—inhibits SHMT expression by blocking direct NRF2–MAFK binding to the SHMT1 promoter and by hindering both the NRF2–ATF4 axis33 and NRF2–MAFK binding to the SHMT2 promoter.
SHMT is required for KL NSCLC survival
Next, to test whether enhanced SHMT activity in KL NSCLC imposes metabolic liabilities, NSCLC cell lines were transfected with SHMT1- or SHMT2-targeting short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) or control siRNA. Owing to the functional redundancy between cytosolic SHMT1 and mitochondrial SHMT2, deletion of a single SHMT isoform has previously been reported to be unsuccessful at impeding cell proliferation under nutrient-replete conditions19–21. Silencing of either SHMT1 or SHMT2, however, readily reduced viability and the time required for cell doubling and increased cell death in KL cell lines, but only marginally affected these factors in K cells (Fig. 3a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b,f,g). Expression of siRNA-resistant SHMT reversed the effects of SHMT silencing in H460 KL cells (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Introducing LKB1 in KL cells almost completely rescued the SHMT-silencing-mediated loss of cell viability and growth defect, confirming that LKB1 status determines SHMT dependence (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 4c,h,j). Using lentiviral CRISPR–Cas9 (CRISPR-V2) to delete SHMT led to increased doubling time, reduced cell viability and anchorage-independent cell growth (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 4i), which was restored by re-expressing SHMT (Extended Data Fig. 4e,k). Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of SHMT using SHIN1 and SHIN2, which are small-molecule SHMT1 and SHMT2 inhibitors20,21, potently suppressed growth and increased death of KL cells, but not K cells; both SHIN1 and SHIN2 effectively blocked SHMT activity, regardless of LKB1 status (Extended Data Fig. 4l–p). Notably, a human lung-tumour tissue microarray detected more SHMT proteins in later stages (stages III and IV) than in stages I and II (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 10a–d), implying that SHMT1 and SHMT2 have an important role in determining NSCLC tumour aggressiveness.
Our observation that the LKB1–SIK1–NRF2 axis is involved in regulation of SHMT gene expression (Fig. 2), and a previous report showing that human KL NSCLCs are highly enriched for loss-of-function mutations in KEAP1, which activate the NRF2 pathway (KLK oncogenotype)36, implied that co-occurrence of KEAP1- and LKB1-inactivating mutations is required for SHMT dependence. Indeed, restoration of either KEAP1 or LKB1 in KL cells rescued the siSHMT1- and siSHMT2-mediated loss of cell viability (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Likewise, co-suppression of KEAP1 and LKB1 sensitized K cells to SHMT silencing more significantly than did suppressing either KEAP1 or LKB1 alone (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Figs. 4r and 5b). In H1373, a K cell line (WT LKB1 and KEAP1), LKB1 knockdown alone is sufficient to sensitize cells to SHIN1 treatment, exhibiting predominant nuclear localization of NRF2, even in the presence of KEAP1 (Fig. 3k), and suggesting that functional KEAP1 loss occurs in these cells. In line with the SHMT dependence of KL cells, SHMT activity was reduced by expression of LKB1 alone, but not KEAP1 alone, and further decreased with co-expression of LKB1 and KEAP1 (Extended Data Fig. 5g,i). Sensitivity of the human KL pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell lines Capan-1 and Capan-2 (ref. 37) to SHMT inhibition was not affected by KEAP1 status (Extended Data Figs. 4q and 5c), indicating that the cell of origin could impact SGOC metabolism. In accordance with gene-regulation data (Fig. 2), deletion of SIK1, but not AMPK or SIK3, rendered cells sensitive to SHMT suppression (Fig. 3l,m and Extended Data Figs. 4s and 5d–f). Constitutively active SIK1 (SIK1 CA) also rescued the SHMT-suppression-mediated loss of cell viability, further supporting the idea that SHMT dependence in KL cells is associated with SIK1 inactivation (Fig. 3n and Extended Data Fig. 4t,u). Taken together, our data suggest that (1) KL cells require SHMT for survival, to a greater extent than K cells do, and (2) the SHMT dependence of KL cells is related to deficiency of both KEAP1 and LKB1 activity (KLK oncogenotype). To further examine the role of SGOC metabolism in KLK settings, we used two isogenic pairs of NSCLC cells with or without LKB1 (H460-EV and H460-LKB1, H1373-shGFP and H1373-shLKB1) as main cell lines, because H460 is a KLK cell line and H1373 is a functional KRAS- and KEAP1-mutant (KK) cell line (Fig. 3k).
SHMT is required for antioxidant defence in KL NSCLC
SHMT controls carbon entry into the one-carbon metabolism pathway, which supports nucleic-acid synthesis, epigenetic regulation, antioxidant defence and amino-acid homeostasis (glycine, serine and methionine) (Fig. 4a). In most proliferating cells, including cancer cells, serine-dependent one-carbon units are necessary for nucleotide production to support growth38–40. In pancreatic tumours with KL mutations, however, one-carbon units are required for DNA methylation18, implying that there is a context-dependent SGOC metabolism requirement. To determine key SGOC-derived metabolic pathway features that are essential for KL NSCLC cell survival and proliferation, we assessed the ability of downstream metabolites (purines and pyrimidines, methyl donors and antioxidants) to rescue cell growth in the context of SHMT suppression. Although neither S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) nor nucleosides restored cell-viability loss, the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) and the reduced form of glutathione (GSH) mitigated the proliferation defects caused by SHMT suppression (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Consistent with the previous pancreatic-tumour study, KL PDAC cells also exhibited sensitivity to SHMT suppression, which was restored by SAM but not GSH, indicating that the cell of origin mediated metabolic dependence (Fig. 4d)18.
Glycine and formate are required for completion of de novo purine biosynthesis when SGOC metabolism is suppressed40. The inability of co-supplementation of glycine and formate to rescue SHMT suppression (Extended Data Fig. 6c) further implies that the functional importance of SHMT in KL NSCLC is associated with the maintenance of redox balance, rather than nucleotide production. Accordingly, both genetic and pharmacological suppression of SHMT significantly increased oxidative stress, which was abrogated by NAC (Fig. 4e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6d–f,l,m). During conditions of oxidative stress, NADPH is oxidized to NADP+ to convert oxidized glutathione (GSSG) into GSH, then GSH is re-oxidized into GSSG to maintain the antioxidant-defence mechanism. Consequently, the NADP+/NADPH and GSSG/GSH ratios increase41. Indeed, we observed significantly higher NADP+/NADPH and of GSSG/GSH ratios in SHMT-suppressed KL cells, but not in their K counterparts (Fig. 4g,h and Extended Data Fig. 6g–k,n–p). Of note, introducing LKB1 alone, but not KEAP1 alone, was sufficient to nullify the increased NADP+/NADPH ratio caused by SHMT inhibition, suggesting that LKB1 status, rather than KEAP1 status, is the driving force causing dependence on SHMT for antioxidant defence (Extended Data Fig. 5h).
Our data raised the question of whether KL mutations promote SGOC-mediated antioxidant production. SGOC metabolism, through the SHMT reaction, contributes to antioxidant defence by producing GSH through the generation of glycine from serine42. However, time-course labelling of [U-13C]serine demonstrated that the GSH-synthesis rate from serine was indistinguishable between control and LKB1-expressing KL cells, as determined by fractional enrichment of 13C-labelled GSH (Fig. 4i). GSH synthesis was readily inhibited by SHMT suppression, regardless of LKB1 status (Extended Data Fig. 6q). Although the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway produces the majority of NADPH43,44, SGOC metabolism has an important role in generating NADPH through methylene tetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase (MTHFD), the first enzyme downstream of SHMT, to manage oxidative stress43,45,46. Notably, silencing MTHFD1 and MTHFD2 reduced cell viability to a level similar to that following SHMT suppression in KL cells, but not in K cells (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), implying that KL mutations might increase SGOC-mediated NADPH synthesis. To test this possibility, we labelled H460 cells with [2,3,3-2H]serine and used proline as a surrogate metabolite, because pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase, a mitochondrial enzyme in the first step in proline biosynthesis, uses NADPH as an electron donor to reduce γ-glutamyl phosphate to Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) (Fig. 4j)19,47. After correcting for the extent of serine labelling and the proline-synthesis rate, about 10% of proline contained a hydrogen from serine at 2 h of labelling, and this increased to ~20% at 12 h of labelling in parental H460 cells. Restoration of LKB1 reduced the transfer of 2H from [2,3,3-2H]serine into proline (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 6t), suggesting that SGOC metabolism contributes significantly to NADPH production in the KL setting. NAD kinase-2 (NADK2), an enzyme that converts NAD(H) to NADP(H) in mitochondria, is essential for maintaining the mitochondrial NADP(H) pool as well as for proline biosynthesis48,49. Silencing NADK2 (in the presence of proline supplementation) selectively reduced KL-cell viability and increased ROS levels (Fig. 4k,l and Extended Data Figs. 6u,v and and 7k). To further validate our findings, an isogenic pair of H460 cells was engineered to express triphosphopyridine nucleotide oxidase (TPNOX) and mitochondrial TPNOX (mitoTPNOX), to decouple the role of SGOC metabolism in NADPH production and nucleotide synthesis. TPNOX is an oxygen-dependent NADPH oxidase that depletes cellular NADPH—both cytosolic and mitochondrial—whereas mitoTPNOX exhausts mitochondrial NADPH by specifically oxidizing mitochondrial NADPH50. Expressing TPNOX and mitoTPNOX increased the doubling time, induced both cellular and mitochondrial oxidative stress in KL cells, but did not do so substantially in K cells (Fig. 4m,n and Extended Data Fig. 7a), supporting our results showing that SGOC metabolism is required for KL cell survival by providing NADPH in the mitochondria.
Our results show that KL cells depend on pools of NAPDH, which they use in antioxidant-defence mechanisms. This raises the question of whether combining SHMT suppression with inhibition of cytosolic NADPH sources could produce a potential synergistic effect. Indeed, combining genetic and pharmacological suppression of key enzymes (G6PD, ME1 and IDH1) in the three main cytosolic-NADPH-generating mechanisms with SHMT inhibition more potently reduced cell growth and increased the NADP+/NADPH ratio in KL cells compared with K cells (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 7b–j).
SHIN2 enhances therapeutic efficacy of paclitaxel in vivo
To determine the impact of SHMT ablation on tumour growth, we used a pool of cells in which SHMT1 and SHMT2 were knocked out using CRISPR (two KL cell lines, H460 and H2122; and two K cell lines, Calu-6 and H1373) for subcutaneous xenograft assays. Of note, although antioxidant supplementation can protect cells from acute SHMT suppression (transient RNA silencing and treatment with SHIN1 and SHIN2), all the metabolites of the SGOC pathway are required for continued proliferation of SHMT-deleted cells. KL tumours from the SHMT1- and SHMT2-KO pools exhibited reduced tumour growth, whereas K tumour growth in the SHMT1- or SHMT2-KO pools barely changed (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b,d). The degree of tumour reduction was associated with KO efficiency within pools; WT or WT-like clones tended to outcompete edited cell populations over time. To circumvent this issue, we generated pools of several KO clones and found that complete deletion of SHMT2 abrogated tumour growth in vivo (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 8c). However, we were unable to obtain a single SHMT1-KO clone (out of more than 300 clones), even with supplementation of all the SGOC metabolites, indicating that SHMT1 is essential for survival of KL NSCLC cells. Given that neither SHMT1 nor SHMT2 is a common essential gene as determined by the Cancer Dependency Map51, and particularly that SHMT1 is not considered a major SHMT isozyme in most cancer cells20,21, further investigation of the underlying mechanism by which SHMT1 is indispensable for KL NSCLC survival is warranted.
Both SHIN1 and SHIN2 have been reported to block SHMT1 and SHMT2 activity in vivo and to have therapeutic efficacy against T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in vivo20,52. To test the in vivo efficacy of SHMT inhibition, we used SHIN1 and SHIN2 in cells in which SHMT was not deleted. Nude mice were subcutaneously injected with three isogenic pairs of NSCLC cell lines with or without LKB1 (H460-EV and H460-LKB1, H2122-EV and H2122-LKB1, H1373-shGFP and H1373-shLKB1) and treated with SHIN1 (100 mg kg−1 body weight, every day) once palpable tumours (80–120 mm3) were present. As previously reported53, KL tumour lines displayed more robust growth in vivo (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 8e). SHIN1 inhibited SHMT activity, as reflected by lower incorporation of 13C into glycine from [U-13C]serine in SHIN1-injected mice than in control mice (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 8f), and attenuated KL tumour growth to a similar level to that in its K counterpart (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly, SHIN2 (200 mg kg−1 body weight, every day) also impaired growth of KL tumour lines (H460 and A549) but not of the K line (Calu-6) (Fig. 5f), although the inhibitor effectively blocked SHMT activity in all tumour lines (Fig. 5g). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining revealed an increase in apoptosis and a decrease in proliferation in KL tumours with SHMT suppression (Fig. 5h–k and Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). In agreement with our in vitro data, SHMT inhibition increased ROS levels in KL tumours (H460 and A549), moreso than in K tumours (Calu-6) (Fig. 5l and Extended Data Fig. 8i). Because of SHIN2’s superior biodistribution in vivo20, it was mainly used in the remaining experiments.
On the basis of our in vitro data, SHMT inhibition was found to disable cells’ ability to maintain redox balance (Fig. 4). To test whether suppressing both GSH synthesis and SHMT activity can reduce tumour growth more effectively, mice were treated with SHIN2 (100 mg kg−1 body weight, half the dose of the previous single treatment, every day) in the presence or absence of buthionine sulfoximine (BSO, 20 mM in drinking water), an inhibitor of glutamate cysteine ligase (GCL), the first enzyme of the GSH biosynthetic pathway. The combination-treatment group showed better tumour reduction and increased ROS levels compared with the single-treatment groups (Fig. 6a,b and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). To further determine whether SHMT suppression enhances the efficacy of ROS-inducing chemotherapeutic agents, SHIN2 was combined with paclitaxel (PTX), a first-line therapeutic in NSCLC that can induce ROS generation through production of extracellular H2O2 from the membrane-associated NADPH oxidase (NOX)54 (Fig. 6c). When their tumour burden reached 80–100 mm3, mice were randomized to treatment with vehicle, SHIN2 alone (100 mg kg−1 body weight, half-dose, every day), PTX alone (10 mg kg−1 body weight, half-dose, every other day) or SHIN2 plus PTX. Although the half dose of either PTX or SHIN2 marginally reduced tumour growth, combination treatment significantly impeded KL tumour growth (Fig. 6c) by decreasing proliferation and increasing apoptosis (Fig. 6d,e). We determined that the combination index of SHMT inhibition with PTX in vivo was between 0.4 and 0.6 by the response additivity metric and around 1 by both the bliss independence and highest single-agent metrics55, indicative of a synergistic effect (Extended Data Fig. 9c and Supplementary Table 8). Subsequent pharmacokinetic analysis revealed that co-administration of PTX and SHIN2 led to significantly higher blood levels of SHIN2 than did administration of SHIN2 as a single agent (Extended Data Fig. 9d). This suggests that PTX and SHIN2 engage in a classical drug–drug interaction in which PTX slows the clearance of SHIN2 by inhibiting hepatic enzymes that are responsible for drug metabolism56. This effect is likely to drive some of the observed synergy between these two agents. Methotrexate (MTX), a DHFR inhibitor that depletes THF pools by using NADPH as an electron donor, enhanced therapeutic efficacy of SHIN2 in only KL (H460) tumours, not in K (Calu-6) tumours (MTX was administered at 10 mg kg−1 body weight twice per week, Extended Data Fig. 9e), whereas treatment with NAC or GSH partially reversed the therapeutic efficacy of the combination treatment on both KL tumour size and ROS levels (Fig. 6f,g and Extended Data Fig. 9f,g). To study the efficacy of SHMT suppression in the context of an intact immune system, we established syngeneic tumour grafts in immunocompetent mice. Of note, there was no clear difference in SHMT dependence between murine KP and KPL NSCLC cells derived from genetically engineered mouse model (GEMM) (Extended Data Fig. 9h), implying that Keap1 loss could be required for SHMT dependence in murine KL NSCLC. Thus, we used Kras-, p53- and Lkb1-mutated (KPL) GEMM-derived cell lines, described in a recent paper by J. Minna’s group57. Keap1 was deleted in these cells, and they (KPLK cells) exhibited a lower half-maximal inhibitory concentration for SHIN2 (0.19 μM) than for that of KPL cells (7.09 μM) (Extended Data Fig. 9i). In a subcutaneous syngeneic mouse model generated through injection of murine KPLK cells, combination treatment also led to superior tumour reduction and increased ROS levels compared with single treatments (Fig. 6h). Finally, to assess the therapeutic efficacy of the combination treatment in more physiologically relevant settings, we established two orthotopic mouse models: NOD-scid IL2Rγnull (NSG) mice with H460 cells (orthotopic xenograft model) and C57BL/6J mice with murine KPLK cells (orthotopic syngeneic model). Mice were subjected to the same treatment scheme that was used for subcutaneous xenografts. Combination treatment reduced proliferation of primary tumours and metastasis in H460 orthotopic mice and increased survival, with more apoptosis in the tumour region, in syngeneic KPLK mice (Fig. 6i and Extended Data Fig. 9j–n).
Discussion
KL NSCLC represents about one-third of mutant-KRAS-driven lung tumours and is associated with poor outcomes owing to resistance to chemotherapy and immune checkpoint therapy58,59. Thus, new treatment modalities for this group of tumours are a pressing need. In this study, we demonstrate that KL tumour survival and proliferation are associated with dependence on SGOC metabolism through SHMT (Fig. 7). By systematically analysing the metabolome of human NSCLC tissues and cell lines and measuring biosynthesis rates of serine and glycine in a highly annotated panel of NSCLC cells, we identified metabolic dependencies in KL NSCLC that were distinct from those in KL PDAC. In both PDAC18 and NSCLC, LKB1 loss in the context of oncogenic KRAS substitutions has a prominent role in the flux of serine entry into one-carbon metabolism; however, the molecular mechanism underlying SGOC activation and dependence in KL NSCLC is different from that in KL PDAC18. SHMT transcription is suppressed in KL NSCLC by LKB1 through SIK, rather than AMPK. This disparity between NSCLC and PDAC could be related to the tumour-suppressive role of SIK in NSCLC. AMPK is amplified in LUAD, and deleting AMPK impedes lung tumorigenesis60 whereas SIK deletion helps lung-cancer growth29,30, indicating that SIK rather than AMPK is the main driver of LKB1-mediated tumour suppression, including SHMT inhibition in NSCLC.
Tumours tend to maintain the metabolic network of the parental tissue, in part through tissue-specific epigenetic regulation61,62. Although further investigation is necessary to understand why NSCLC requires SGOC metabolism for redox homeostasis rather than epigenetic regulation, as is the case in PDAC, it could be related to the physiological role of the lung. The lung is the foundational organ of the respiratory system, facilitating gas exchange between the environment and the bloodstream. Thus, constant exposure to oxygen can lead to a higher basal demand on redox-stress-defence mechanisms, which in turn can be further activated in NSCLC. This might also explain the high frequency of somatic mutations in KEAP1 and NRF2 in NSCLC. Tumours with KEAP1 loss and NRF2 activation mitigate oxidative stress by inducing various enzymes that produce cytosolic NADPH63,64. Our findings demonstrate that KEAP1 loss and NRF2 activation in KLK NSCLC also increase SGOC-derived NADPH production by increasing direct NRF2–MAFK binding to AREs in SHMT promoter regions. It supports a previous study that suggested that NRF2 regulates SGOC gene expression combinatorially through ATF4 and additional factors (but not PHGDH)33. Although it remains to be elucidated how SIK inhibits NRF2–MAFK-mediated transactivation of SHMT, one possibility is that direct phosphorylation of MAFK or NRF2 impedes binding to SHMT promoter regions. SIK phosphorylates substrates that contain the sequence (L,I,V)X(R,K)XX(S,T)XXX(L,I,V)65; we noted this consensus motif in MAFK, implying that it could be the direct downstream target of SIK. Although beyond the scope of the current study, it will be interesting to determine whether SIK alters chromatin accessibility of global antioxidant-responsive genes regulated by NRF2–MAFK, rather than just SHMT.
Most proliferating cells, including cancer cells and lymphocytes, have been known to require SGOC metabolism for nucleotide synthesis to support growth38,40. In this case, however, SGOC metabolism provides metabolites that are important for redox balance. This can explain why supplementation of formate and glycine rescued cell-viability loss in the previous studies40,66, but not in KL NSCLC. Under SHMT suppression, one-carbon units from formate can bypass 5,10-methylene-THF deprivation and generate formyl-THF for nucleotide (purine) synthesis, and they can generate NADP+ and potentially deplete NADPH through MTHFD (Fig. 2b). The essential role of the SHMT–MTHFD axis in NADPH production in SGOC metabolism could also explain in part why single gene deletion (SHMT1 or SHMT2) is detrimental to KL NSCLC, whereas most cancers do not exhibit SHMT dependence unless both forms are perturbed.
SHMT inhibition by SHIN1 and SHIN2 has shown efficacy at treating blood cancers20,21. Our data, for the first time to our knowledge, demonstrate that SHIN2, especially when combined with PTX, can also effectively reduce solid tumour growth. In summary, we provide a rationale and therapeutic strategy in which combining SGOC inhibition with a ROS-inducing agent could open new avenues for the treatment of a highly aggressive lung-cancer type. Given that distinct metabolic vulnerabilities have been observed in NSCLC and PDAC18, even with the same driver mutations, our work reinforces the notion that a deep understanding of the interaction between cell of origin and genetic events should precede selection of the right treatment approaches.

ChIP–qPCR
ChIP experiments were performed as previously described67, with modifications. Briefly, 2 × 106–5 × 106 cells were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 5 min at room temperature. After overnight incubation, protein A Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, no. 10002D) were added to the ChIP reactions and incubated for 4 additional hours at 4 °C to collect the immunoprecipitated chromatin. Subsequently, Dynabeads were washed twice with 1 ml of RIPA buffer, twice with 1 ml of RIPA buffer with 0.3 M NaCl, twice with 1 ml of LiCl buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.5% NP-40, 250 mM LiCl, pH 8.0) and twice with 1 ml TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0). Chromatin was eluted in SDS elution buffer (1% SDS, 10 mM EDTA, 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0) followed by reverse crosslinking at 65 °C overnight. ChIP DNA was treated with RNaseA (5 μg ml−1) and protease K (0.2 mg ml−1), and purified using QIAquick Spin Columns (Qiagen). Purified ChIP DNA was quantified by real-time PCR using the iQ SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad). ATAC-seq

In brief, 5 × 104 cells were resuspended in 50 μl lysis buffer (10 mM Tris pH7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 0.1% NP-40 and Complete Protease inhibitor (Roche)) and spun at 500g for 10 min at 4 °C to collect nuclei. Cell metabolomics
To compare metabolites between A549-EV and A549-LKB1 cells, cells were plated at 3 × 106 cells per 10 cm plate for 16 h before collection. Two hours before collection, cells were incubated with fresh medium. At the time of collection, cells were washed with ice-cold saline, lysed with an 80:20 ratio of methanol to water and quickly scraped into an Eppendorf tube, followed by three freeze–thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen. The insoluble material was pelleted in a cooled centrifuge (4 °C), and the supernatant was transferred to a new tube and evaporated until dry using a SpeedVac concentrator (Eppendorf). Metabolites were reconstituted in 100 μl of 0.03% formic acid in liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS)-grade water, mixed by vortexing and centrifuged to remove debris. Samples were randomized and blinded before LC–MS/MS analysis. LC–MS/MS and data acquisition were performed using an Applied Biosystems QTRAP 5500 liquid chromatography/triple quadrupole mass spectrometer with an injection volume of 20 μl. Chromatogram review and peak area integration were performed using the MultiQuant software v.2.1 (Applied Biosystems), and the peak area for each detected metabolite was normalized by two methods: (1) one against the total ion count, and (2) another against the protein amount of the sample to correct any variations introduced from sample handling through instrument analysis. A side-by-side comparison is shown in Supplementary Tables 1–5. The normalized areas were used as variables for the multivariate and univariate statistical data analysis. All multivariate analyses and modelling on the normalized data were carried out using MetaboAnalyst v.5.0 (http://www.metaboanalyst.ca). Univariate statistical differences in the metabolites between two groups were analysed using a two-tailed Student’s t-test.

The samples were reconstituted with 200 μl of an 80:20 ratio of acetonitrile to water, and the insoluble material was pelleted in a cooled centrifuge (4 °C). The supernatant was then diluted 10–20 times with an 80:20 ratio of acetonitrile to water. Samples were analysed using a SCIEX QTRAP 6500 liquid chromatograph/triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. We performed separation of metabolites on a SeQuant zic-pHILIC polymeric HPLC column (150 × 2 mm) in a Nexera Ultra-High-Performance Liquid Chromatograph system (Shimadzu Corporation). Mobile-phase solvents were 10 mM ammonium acetate aqueous (pH 9.8, adjusted with ammonia water (A), and pure acetonitrile (B)). The elution gradient was: 0–15 min, linear gradient 90–30% B, 10–70% A; 15–18 min, 30% B, 70% A; 18–19 min, linear gradient 30–90% B, 70–10% A. Then, the column was reconditioned for 6 min using 90% B and 10% A. The flow rate was 0.25 ml min−1, and the column was operated at 40 °C. Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) was used to monitor NEM-derived GSH (Glu-Cys(NEM)-Gly) and the glycine-truncated fragment (Glu-Cys(NEM), 433/358, CE, 26V). The corresponding transitions used for different isotopomers were: M + 0 (433/358), M + 1 (434/358, 434/359), M + 2 (435/358, 435/359, 435/360), M + 3 (436/359, 436/360, 436/362), M + 4 (437/360, 437/361, 437/362), M + 5 (438/361, 438/362, 438/363), M + 6 (439/362, 439/363, 439/364), M + 7 (440/363, 440/364, 440/365), M + 8 (441/364, 441/365, 441/366), M + 9 (442/365, 442/366) and M + 10 (443/366). The [1,2-13C] glycine-containing GSH isotopomers were distinguished as 435/358, 436/359, 437/360, 438/361, 439/362, 440/363, 441/364, 442/365 and 443/366. The fractional enrichment of [1,2-13C]glycine-containing GSH isotopomers was obtained by dividing the total values of the above transitions by the values of the total of all 27 transitions.
In vivo infusion
Infusions were performed when flank tumours were 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter. Mice were fasted the night before the infusion for about 12 h, and the next day, [U-13C]serine was infused for 8 h at a rate of 0.324 mg kg−1 body weight per min, with a total dose of 155.5 mg kg−1 body weight in 960 μl saline. Blood samples (10 μl) were collected at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 h through retro-orbital bleeding. Animals were euthanized at the end of the infusion, and tumours were collected and frozen in liquid nitrogen. Frozen tissues were then weighed and divided into three fragments for technical replicates. Fragments were homogenized in extraction solvent (50:50 methanol to water) and processed and analysed as described above (in the ‘Stable-isotope tracing assays for measuring the rate of serine–glycine biosynthesis’ section).
Mouse xenografts and tumour-tissue assays
Animal procedures were performed with the approval of the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC) and Yale School of Medicine (YSM) Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees. Mice were euthanized before reaching one of the following humane end points, in accordance with UIC and YSM guidelines: (1) tumour size greater than 2 cm in diameter; (2) tumour size exceeding 15% of the preoperative body weight, as estimated by the formula volume (mm3) = (length (mm) × width (mm)2) / 2 and assuming a tumour density of 1 g cm−3, therefore assuming 1 mm3 = 1 mg; (3) >20% net loss of body weight; or (4) tumour ulceration. Cells (0.1 × 106 EV-H460; 0.1 × 106 EV-H2122; 1 × 106 LKB1-H460; 1 × 106 LKB1-H2122; 1 × 106 shGFP-expressing H1373; 1 × 106 shLKB1-expressing H1373; Calu-6, 3 × 106 A549; 3 × 106 KPLK) were suspended in serum-free RPMI and mixed with Matrigel (Corning, no. 356237) at a 1:1 ratio. For the SHMT-KO study, cells were implanted subcutaneously into 6-week-old athymic nude-Foxn1nu mice (Envigo and Taconic). For the SHIN1 and SHIN2 study, 10-week-old mice were used. To generate syngeneic xenografts, 6-week-old C57BL/6N mice (The Jackson Laboratory) were used. After tumour-cell injection, mice were randomized to treatments and then divided into cages. For drug treatment, tumour-bearing mice were intraperitoneally injected with vehicle (for single-treatment experiments in Fig. 5d,e and Supplementary Fig. 8e: 20% DMSO, 30% Cremophor EL (Sigma-Aldrich, no. 238470), 50% water; for combination-treatment experiments in Fig. 6a,c,f,g,h and Supplementary Fig. 9a,e,g,h: 12% DMSO, 18% Cremophor EL, 70% water), SHIN1 (single dose: 100 mg kg−1 body weight, half dose: 50 mg kg−1 body weight), SHIN2 (single dose: 200 mg kg−1 body weight, half dose: 100 mg kg−1 body weight) and/or PTX (MCE, no. HY-B0015, 10 mg kg−1 body weight), methotrexate (Research Products International, no. M63820, 10 mg kg−1 body weight) and BSO (20 mM in drinking water) after mice presented palpable tumours (~80–100 mm3). Tumour size was measured every other day using electronic calipers.
Orthotopic xenograft and syngeneic model
Animal procedures were performed with the approval of UTSW IACUC. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size, but our sample sizes were determined on the basis of our previous publications22,23. The protocol for orthotopic lung transplantation of cancer cells has been previously described70. In brief, 8- to 12-week-old NSG or C57BL/6J mice were anaesthetized with metered isoflurane. Mice were placed in a biosafety cabinet, and the left side of the chest was shaved and sterilized with povidone-iodine and then 70% ethanol. A~1-cm incision was made in the skin and subcutaneous fat, and the left chest wall and lung were visualized. Next, 0.1 × 106 cells of H460 cells or 0.5 × 106 murine KPLK cells expressing firefly luciferase in 25% matrigel (Corning, no. 356237) and PBS were injected between the ribs, directly into the left lung. The skin incision was closed with two staples, and intraperitoneal carboprofen 5 mg kg−1 body weight was administered after the procedure and then daily for 2 more days. Tumours were imaged by bioluminescence imaging (BLI) on an AMI-HTX (Spectral Instruments Imaging) in the Small Animal Imaging Resource (SAIR) 1 week after tumour-cell transplantation and on treatment days 9, 16, 22 and 27. Mice were treated with intraperitoneal injections as described for the subcutaneous xenograft experiments, except a full dose of SHIN2 (Fig. 6c). Tissue samples from the experiment were processed, and paraffin blocks were generated by the Tissue Management (TM) core facility at UTSW. The SAIR and TM core facilities are supported in part by an NCI Cancer Center Support Grant (P30CA142543).
Pharmacokinetic analysis
Pharmacokinetic analysis of SHIN2 and PTX was carried out in 6- to 8-week-old female CD1 mice (n = 3 per group). The compounds were dissolved in a vehicle solution consisting of 12% DMSO, 18% Cremophor EL and 70% water at 20 mg ml−1 (SHIN2) or 2 mg ml−1 (PTX). Compounds were administered by intraperitoneal injection, and blood was collected from the dorsal metatarsal vein (at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12 h after injection) or terminal cardiac puncture (24 h after injection) into heparin tubes. Plasma was collected from these samples, and 10 μl plasma was mixed with 150 μl acetonitrile containing dexamethasone as an internal standard. These samples were vortexed for 30 s and centrifuged at 4000 r.p.m. for 15 min at 4 °C to precipitate protein, and the supernatant was diluted in water before LC–MS analysis. SHIN2 and PTX concentrations in the plasma samples were determined by comparison to standard curves prepared in blank plasma.
Human NSCLC tissue microarray
A tissue microarray (TMA) with 210 human NSCLC samples (University of Kentucky) was unidentified and probed with antibodies against SHMT1 (Sigma-Aldrich, no. HPA023314) and SHMT2 (CST, no. 33443). Immunohistochemistry analysis was performed in A Leica Bond Max (Leica Biosystem) with an antibody dilution of 1:200 (1 h) for SHMT1, and 1:400 (1 h) for SHMT2. Staining intensity was graded as: 0 (no staining); 1+ (weak staining); 2+ (moderate staining); and 3+ (intense staining), then reviewed by two pathologists independently. The scoring system was based on intensity and percent staining. For SHMT1 and SHMT2, the expression score was calculated by multiplying percentage (0 = 0, 1 = 1–25%, 2 = 25–75%, 3 ≥ 75%) by intensity (weak = 1, moderate = 2, strong = 3). If the product was negative, the score was 0; if the product was <3, the score was 1+; if the product was ≥3 but <6, the score was 2+; and if the product was ≥6, the score was 3+. After TMA scoring, the samples were re-identified, and results were interpreted. TMA research was supported by the Biospecimen Procurement & Translational Pathology Shared Resource Facility of the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center (P30CA177558).
Tumour-tissue staining and TUNEL assay
After mice were euthanized, whole tumour tissues were collected, and about one-third of the tissues was formalin fixed and paraffin embedded (5-μm thickness). To measure proliferation in tumour tissues, tissues were stained with an antibody to Ki67 (Proteintech, 27309-1-AP) at the UIC Research Histology and Tissue Imaging Core. Images were acquired using a Leica DMi8 microscope, and Ki67+ cells and the total number of cells per tumour were quantified using Matlab. In brief, images were converted from RGB to hue-saturation-value (purity-vibrancy-brightness, HSV), and the HSV values were examined. Two independent filters based on HSV values, one filter highlighting only H&E-stained cells (blue) and the other filter highlighting only Ki67+ cells (brown and blue), were then created, and the total number of blue and brown stained cells for each image was calculated. Cell death was detected in xenografts using the In Situ Cell Death Detection kit, Fluorescein (Roche, no. 11684809910) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, tissue sections were deparaffinized with xylene and rehydrated with ethanol. After being washed in PBS, tissue sections were incubated with blocking buffer (10% normal goat serum in 10% BSA, Vector Laboratories, S-1000–20), followed by reaction solution for 1 h at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere in the dark. Cellular ROS levels were detected in xenografts using the CM-H2DCFDA (Invitrogen). Briefly, tissue sections were incubated with blocking buffer, followed by 20 μM DCFDA solution for 1 h at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere in the dark. Finally, DAPI was added to the tissue sections for nuclei staining (Thermo Fisher Scientific, no. P36931), and coverslips were applied. Images were acquired using a Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM700), and TUNEL+ cells and total cells per tumour were quantified using Matlab. In brief, two independent filters based on blue–green values, one filter highlighting only DAPI-stained cells (blue) and the other filter highlighting only TUNEL+ cells (green), were then created, and the total number of blue and green stained cells for each image was calculated.
FACS analysis for ROS in tumour tissues
After mice were euthanized, whole tumour tissues were collected, and about one-fifth of the tissues was minced and then incubated with RPMI-1640 containing collagenase IV (Gibco, no. 17104019), Hyaluronidase (Sigma-Aldrich, no. H3506) and DNase I (Invitrogen, no. 18068015) at 37 °C for 30 min. Digested tumour tissues were transferred into a 40-μm strainer (BD falcon, 352340) and centrifuged at 300g at room temperature for 10 min. After being washed 3 times with PBS, digested tumour tissues were resuspended in PBS containing 1 μM CM-H2DCFDA, then incubated for 30 min at 37 °C in the dark. As a negative control, Alexa-Flour-488-conjugated goat anti-mouse-IgG was used. After being washed with PBS, digested tumour tissues were analysed by flow cytometry (CytoFLEX). Data analysis was performed using FlowJo V10.
Statistics
The data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested in all experiments. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v.10 or IBM SPSS statistics v.27. For statistical comparisons of two conditions with equal variances, a two-tailed Student’s t-test was performed. For statistical comparisons of two conditions with unequal variances (for example, H460 in Fig. 3b), a two-tailed Welch’s unequal variances t-test were used. For comparisons of more than two groups, data were analysed with a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparisons post hoc test (except in Fig. 5e, in which Sidak’s post hoc test was used). To calculate the significance for repeated measurements over time, a two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparisons post hoc test was used. For association analysis between tumour stages and SHMT expression (Fig. 3h), a two-tailed Fisher’s exact test was performed. Statistical analyses are further described in Supplementary Table 6.
